title: The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build
summary:
Agility Robotics, the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5. It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do.

Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined.

From ATRIAS to Digit

My dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals.

We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS—short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait.

With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be?

Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones, and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie.

Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard, Caltech, the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them.

ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year.Agility Robotics

Because Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion: A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash.

Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1, which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers.

Why Digit Began With Warehouse Bins

As we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers.

After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins. Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. Because the task can vary widely from one deployment to another, it hasn’t been broadly addressed by single-purpose automation. Yet it was constrained enough to give Digit an economically viable first job while it developed a broader set of skills.

In 2019, Digit began demonstrating its capabilities to do real work. With Ford Motor Company, we showed how Digit 1 could carry packages from an autonomous vehicle to a front porch. We developed Digit 2 and 3 while working with a certain global package delivery company on moving and sorting cardboard boxes. Amazon tested Digit 4 on moving and stacking bins, and it became the world’s first commercially deployed humanoid at the logistics provider GXO. In 2024, Digit appeared on the cover of Time magazine.

Despite Digit’s apparent success, we began to run into conflicts between my dream and the needs of actual customers. We were no longer working with relatively patient university research labs. Agility has to sell robots to survive, and customers will only purchase robots that provide value. If bins weren’t moving, our customers were losing money. We spent a huge amount of time and effort keeping our first deployments operational, which arguably eliminated any profit we made. Yet this also kept our company learning and alive the way no lab demo ever could.

I had no idea how hard it would be, or that running a company would involve so many things that have nothing to do with solving technical problems: deployments across the country; shipping, service, and customer support; fundraising and investor relations; more fundraising; human resources and IT; developing fleet-management software; managing a supply chain; and even more fundraising. I had no experience with any of these things. My career had focused on solving the technical challenges of robots interacting with the world, and it turned out that was only a tiny piece of building a successful robotics company. But Agility was the only path I saw to continuing the technical work and having an impact.

Turning Digit Into a Product

I knew that Agility needed to focus more on robots as a product, but I didn’t know how to make that happen. Hiring the people we needed to run the company meant giving up an immense amount of control, but we had no other choice. We recruited a new executive team with the experience required to commercialize this new technology, and they quickly made changes that were both painful and necessary.

Digit versions 1, 2, and 3 [left to right] show the evolution of the robot from a dynamic walking platform into a useful mobile manipulator. Agility

We had intended the next revision of Digit, Digit 4 EVT (Engineering Validation and Test), to be a relatively minor upgrade. But Agility’s new leadership insisted that the robot was missing key features that were essential if Digit was going to become a real product. So Digit 4 EVT instead incorporated a series of major changes in a highly compressed timeline, such as larger batteries and system-wide upgrades for safety and regulatory compliance, which added enough mass to dramatically alter the robot’s appearance and capabilities.

While early Digits were headless, Agility Robotics was able to justify a head for Digit 4 to optimize antenna and camera placement, and it turned out to be surprisingly useful for human-robot interaction.Christie Hemm Klok

I could only watch as others brought their own talents to bear to make Digit into a successful product, in gut-wrenching ways that didn’t always align with my vision. There were some especially difficult times when I felt like there were compromises made that didn’t seem necessary, but making those decisions was no longer my sole responsibility. I had to accept that Digit had grown far beyond me, and look for ways of influencing decisions rather than directing them. In the moment, it was incredibly frustrating, as Digit 4 EVT took a few steps backward from my vision of how humanoids should look and move.

Agility is in our name because agility is core to the future of the company. I want Digit to be lithe and graceful. When people see Digit, I want them to like the robot, to understand what it can do at a glance, and to feel that it’s there to help. But with Digit 4 EVT, all of that was sacrificed to functionality, because of course it had to be—the customer just needs the robot to do the work. The design process became a ruthless triage, with aesthetics and elegance of movement being delayed over and over again in favor of brutal functionality. For an engineer whose mind lives more in the future than in the present, it has been hard for me to accept this trajectory. And yet, through Digit 4 EVT’s commercial deployments, we began to really understand specific applications and what they required. We mapped the first 10 use cases Digit would perform, and then began designing Digit 5 from scratch based on everything we had learned.

Digit 5

Digit 5 will be Agility’s first real step toward a general-purpose robot. It marks our transition from imagining what a future humanoid robot should be to designing a product around the realities of customer deployments. These realities include things like European CE regulatory compliance, North American UL electrical-safety certifications, and Federal Communications Commission limits for electromagnetic radiation—all of which felt tangential to my dream for Digit, but were absolute requirements.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers while working 20 hours a day and lifting more than a human can.Christie Hemm Klok

Customer requirements helped us realize that safety in particular was one of the most critical barriers to scaling. In Digit 4’s commercial deployments, the robots had to work behind physical barriers, separated from humans at all times, to meet insurance and regulatory demands. This seemed silly to me, because I’ve never felt that our robots were dangerous, but we have to prove that they’re safe. And since keeping the robots in safety cages severely limited their usefulness, enabling Digit 5 to operate safely around people became a primary design goal. We spent two years on this challenge.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers. It will rely on an array of sensors to locate nearby people in a manner that’s certifiably safe, and then take actions based on that information. As a person approaches, Digit 5 is programmed to stop what it’s doing, set down its payload, sit on the floor, and cut power to its motors before the person gets close enough to touch the robot. This conservative approach reduces the risk to nearby people in a verifiable way, and we believe it’s the only approach that makes sense as a first step toward working alongside humans.

Yet this strategy also feels like a massive slowdown on the path toward robots becoming part of everyday life. Enabling coexistence with humans has influenced almost every aspect of Digit 5’s design: the shape of the legs and the body, the safety-rated sensors within protective housings, the isolated computers dedicated to safety, and more. All of these features increase the robot’s complexity, power consumption, mass, and physical size.

Digit 5 is Agility’s largest, heaviest, strongest, and most capable humanoid robot worker.

The robot’s design was driven by safety, with integrated protection for the robot and for the humans it will work around.Agility Robotics

Weighing over 120 kg, Digit 5 is a huge robot. It needed to achieve the lifting limits recommended under the U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health guidelines for human workers, which include repeatedly lifting 23-kg bins and reaching shelves 1.75 meters high. Digit is designed to perform tasks like these for 20 hours a day—something no human can do. This requires motors with enough power and torque to lift the load, but also enough precision to delicately control the force Digit applies when it makes contact with the world. To power those motors, we needed a large battery and a dock for rapid autonomous charging. The dock will deliver 240 amperes at 48 volts, which is enough current to make its thick charging cables visibly wiggle under the induced magnetic forces, while powerful fans blow air through cooling channels in the robot’s torso to keep the battery from overheating. The battery and cooling system takes up about 75 percent of Digit’s torso, but it will allow the robot to operate for 90 minutes and fully recharge during a 9-minute break, enabling near-continuous work.

All of this extra bulk means that Digit 5 can no longer run or jump the way previous generations could, and the svelte form I imagined has become physically impossible. In some ways, Digit 5 feels more like a forklift than the graceful humanoid I set out to build. But looking at the situation rationally, I believe this trade-off is necessary for any company that claims its humanoid can do this kind of work today: If you see a robot that looks like a human working in a factory or warehouse, it either can’t lift the required weight or can’t make it through the whole shift. And if it’s not covered with sensors, it’s likely not safe to stand next to.

The most visible change with Digit 5 is that humanlike legs replace the ostrichlike legs of our earlier versions. While the “backward” leg configuration was optimized for walking and running, we discovered that it created problems with squatting because the ankle will strike the ground. Digit 5 will spend a lot of time lifting heavy objects from near the floor, so we used a humanoid leg configuration with knee and hip motors that both contribute torque to help the robot stand up again.

When Digit detects an approaching human, the robot will lower itself to the floor and cut power to its motors. Agility believes this is the only near-term approach to verifiably reduce risk when the robot is working near people.Agility Robotics

Other companies building humanoid robots have copied the human form without ever understanding its purpose. It’s very frustrating that, to an outside observer, it now looks like we discarded Agility’s distinctive leg design and simply did what everyone else was doing. Yet I know that we arrived at this shape based purely on functional engineering choices. Making a robot look like a human is the easy part—without the function to match, and the understanding of the physics underlying that function, the whole point of the human form may be lost.

With the power, battery life, and safety features that we are designing into Digit 5, we will have a truly useful robot. But it also compromises on some things that are core to my vision and mission. I understand why we made the choices we did and can justify them all, but together they leave me unsatisfied. It’s the curse of the engineer.

What Comes After Digit 5

I believe Digit 5 will be the scaling moment for Agility Robotics, the inflection point where we can begin deploying robots in large numbers. While the robot will continue carrying bins, our road map includes many more tasks, from picking individual items and tending machines, to preparing parts for assembly and shipping, and eventually doing assembly work itself. Its interchangeable tool interfaces and modular design will enable us to gradually upgrade its subsystems. It will be a platform for improvement, a source of data for future behavior training, and a viable product all at the same time.

Hurst stands between the previous version of Digit, Digit 4 EVT [left], and Digit 5.Christie Hemm Klok

But I cannot love Digit 5. It’s the largest, heaviest, most expensive robot Agility will ever build, full of design compromises that enable it to be exactly the robot it needs to be right now rather than the robot I dreamed of. In the beginning, I envisioned steady progress on agility and dexterity, with each version becoming more dynamically capable. Instead, developing Digit 5 has required large detours to incorporate requirements that seemed unrelated to my original vision. However, I now recognize that tackling these challenges was always necessary. Customers and product requirements didn’t ruin my vision; they revealed what my vision was missing. This is how robots will achieve commercial success and make a real-world impact, which will bring me closer to my scientific dream as well.

We won’t have a humanoid that matches the capabilities of humans until it achieves that mastery of motion that inspired me to found Agility over a decade ago. I saw glimmers of it with the spring-mass locomotion of ATRIAS, and more glimmers with Cassie’s running gait.

I know that such mastery is physically possible with the tools and hardware that we have right now, and despite all of its compromises, Digit 5 will give us a practical foundation for pursuing that dream. I want every future version of Digit to be lighter and more graceful, to interact more naturally with humans, and to be better at manipulating objects and moving through the world, enabling robots to enter aspects of our lives that they haven’t been able to help with before. By the time I’m old enough to need assistance at home, I expect Digit will be up to the task.

With Digit 5, Agility has built a robot that will be useful in our world. Now I’m getting back to work to make it beautiful, too.

summary:
Video Friday is your weekly selection of awesome robotics videos, collected by your friends at IEEE Spectrum robotics. We also post a weekly calendar of upcoming robotics events for the next few months. Please send us your events for inclusion.

CoRL 2026: 9–12 November 2026, AUSTIN
Humanoids 2026: 6–9 December 2026, SANTA CLARA, CA

Enjoy today’s videos!

When one robot loves another robot very much, and they’re connected by a wire, they can get together and make a brand new robot! SFW.

[ JSK Lab ]

What happens when Microducks meet? They start to sing together. Each Microduck syncs with its neighbors over Bluetooth, then they compose a song on the fly, in harmony and in perfect time. There’s no score and no conductor. Two, three, or four ducks are enough for a choir to break out.

If Pollen isn’t selling Microducks in four packs for this exact reason, WHAT ARE THEY EVEN DOING!?

[ Pollen ]

In an internal test, Google DeepMind robotics researchers instructed Gemini 4 Argon to watch a video of a human playing cornhole. Using its video understanding and advanced reasoning capabilities, Gemini 4 built a virtual simulation in MuJoCo and accurately calculated the physics and whole-body control required for Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid to sink seven consecutive shots in the real world. This Video-to-Sim-to-Real pipeline compresses weeks of manual modeling into a few hours, transforming ordinary videos into an infinite training ground for physical AI.

[ Google DeepMind ]

As of 11 October 2026, NASA’s Perseverance rover has driven 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers), becoming the new off-world record-holder for total distance driven by any vehicle on the surface of another world. The previous record of 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers) was held by NASA’s Opportunity rover. Perseverance reached that mark on the 2,006th Martian day, or sol, of its mission, covering in five and a half years a distance that took Opportunity almost 15.

[ JPL ]

Let’s not argue about whether these are robots or not and just agree that they’re cool.

[ OATs ]

If one cute little robot can clean up one block, how many blocks can 40 cute little robots clean up? Science has the answers!

[ Paper ]

Thanks, Keisuke!

Before Rosalind Franklin can explore Mars, it has to get off its lander. Engineers are rehearsing that first journey on Earth, using a full-size rover model and Mars-like terrain. The test recreates some of the challenges Rosalind Franklin will face on the Red Planet, from reduced gravity and a 20-degree incline to uneven ground and obstacles beneath its ramps.

[ European Space Agency ]

From custom part to running robot, the Atlas shop floor is built on precision, rapid assembly, and real-time collaboration. By machining parts in-house and streamlining assembly and repair under one roof, we are driving the manufacturing velocity needed to turn complex designs into walking hardware at scale.

[ Boston Dynamics ]

What can a quadruped robot do beyond the lab? Deep in China’s Ailao Mountains, DEEP Robotics Lynx M20S joined a team of researchers on a biodiversity field expedition—navigating rugged terrain, scouting routes ahead, carrying research equipment, and capturing wildlife in areas that are difficult to access on foot.

[ DEEP Robotics ]

The Kamino simulation software is a GPU-accelerated physics solver designed for accurate simulation of complex mechanical systems with kinematic loops, such as parallel manipulators, planar and spatial linkages, and multi-limbed robots with coupled joints, without requiring simplified approximations.

[ Disney Research ]

The original Kawasaki UNIMATE robot as featured in (remember this show?) The MacNeil/Lehrer Report in 1982.

WildOS enables autonomous robots to perform long-range, open-vocabulary object search in previously unmapped and unstructured outdoor environments by unifying geometric safety with semantic visual reasoning. Through a vision-scored navigation graph and beyond-horizon target localization, the system demonstrates more efficient and robust exploration than conventional geometric or purely vision-based approaches in extensive field experiments.

[ ETH Zurich Robotics Systems Lab ]

Who needs an AI-generated person when you can have an actual robot that looks exactly like an AI-generated person instead?

The recovery behaviors here are impressive, but the robot is far slower than a human would be, suggesting that the value it generates is primarily in novelty. Which is fine for now, but novelty wears off, and then what?

title: Q&A: Mars Perseverance Rover Sets a Distance Record
summary:
On 11 October, the Perseverance rover completed a drive that brought its total distance traveled on Mars to 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers). This is a new record for Mars rovers, enabled in large part by Perseverance’s ability to drive with much more autonomy than its predecessors. Over the past five years, Perseverance’s autonomy software has been steadily upgraded, and to learn more about how the record was broken and what the future holds for the rover, we spoke with Mark Maimone, the Perseverance Robotic Operations Deputy Team Chief at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, who designed and developed the self-driving software for Mars rovers Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, and Perseverance.

Before we talk about Perseverance, let’s pour one out for the previous record holder, Opportunity, which landed on Mars in January 2004 for a three-month mission and ended its epic journey 15 years later in February 2019. This NASA video compresses Opportunity’s entire mission into four minutes and gives a poignant sense of the incredible distance that this little rover traveled over its 15-year life on Mars, doing science as it went:

NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory/YouTube

Opportunity drove 45.16 kilometers until a planetary-scale dust storm stopped it in its tracks, appropriately enough, in Perseverance Valley.

On 18 February 2021, Perseverance joined NASA’s Curiosity rover on the red planet, carrying the Ingenuity helicopter tucked under its belly. Curiosity and Perseverance both ditched Opportunity’s solar panels for a radioisotope thermoelectric generator. Curiosity has been active on Mars since 2012.

Despite Curiosity’s nearly 10-year head start, Perseverance is the rover to first break Opportunity’s record. There are several reasons for Perseverance overtaking Opportunity—ruggedized wheels for one—but the biggest contributor is that Perseverance was built for autonomy.

Maimone shares how JPL added enough autonomy for its Mars rover to drive itself from 225 million km away without crashing.

This animation shows Perseverance’s point of view during a drive of 807 feet (246 meters) along the rim of Jezero Crater on 10 December 2025, the 1,709th Martian day, or sol, of the mission. Captured over 2 hours and 35 minutes, 53 Navigation Camera (Navcam) image pairs were combined with rover data on orientation, wheel speed, and steering angle, as well as data from Perseverance’s Inertial Measurement Unit, and placed into a 3D virtual environment. The result is this reconstruction with virtual frames inserted about every 4 inches (0.1 meters) of drive progress. JPL-Caltech/NASA

Let’s talk about rover autonomy on Mars. Even before Perseverance, rovers were driving themselves, right?

Mark Maimone: Yes! Sojourner [in 1997] had an early kind of autonomous behavior—for sensing, it used four laser stripes projected onto the surface, which it used to measure the height of 20 points in the terrain in front of it. It could steer around big obstacles, or even thread the needle between two things. It was a real autonomy system, which is very impressive considering its CPU was less than one megahertz.

With Spirit and Opportunity, I developed the autonomy for those rovers. Every time they drove, they would use 256 x 256 pixel stereo pairs to map the geometry of the terrain and find a safe route forward. Spirit actually ended up driving itself 23 percent of the time, which I was frankly shocked by, since it drove much more slowly in that mode. But using autonomy helped Spirit travel 50 percent faster than it otherwise could have. Opportunity and Curiosity both only used autonomous driving about 5 percent of the time. Perseverance is the first Mars rover that drives itself 90 percent of the time, with its enhanced autonomy system that includes a second processor with an FPGA to speed up extra image processing operations.

What was it like to let Perseverance drive itself for the first time?

Maimone: Perseverance is the culmination of decades of work on Mars rover autonomy, so seeing Perseverance use its AutoNav system to drive itself basically at full speed, up to 120 meters an hour, was incredible.

These two images taken by Perseverance’s hazard avoidance and navigation cameras show (at left) the very first AutoNav drive on Mars where the rover autonomously stopped before running into a rock pile, and (at right) the second AutoNav drive where the rover successfully steered around a rock.JPL-Caltech/NASA

Where are the humans in this process?

Maimone: The plan of where to go is specified by the science team, and then on the engineering side, the strategic route planning team develops a path to get us to that goal by guessing, based on lower-resolution maps from orbit, what the terrain is going to look like for the rover. Each day, a tactical operations team combines the strategic overall route with that day’s science goals to pick the actual route the rover will follow.

We want humans to keep doing long-range planning because that avoids wasting time. For example, we’ve learned that if we see sandy areas with intersecting waves or crests—not just ripples blown in one direction, but cross-ripples going in multiple directions—the rover tends to sink into terrain like that, so we tell the rover to keep out of those areas. The onboard autonomy only measures terrain shape, not terrain type, so it benefits from those location-based annotations.

We now have years of experience correlating images taken from orbit with images taken by the rover, and understanding how different kinds of terrain affect the drive. With the current orbiters at Mars, we sometimes get 25 centimeters resolution on orbital images. That’s still not quite enough to see all obstacles; there could be a big rock that doesn’t really show up on a scale of more than one or two pixels, making it very hard to notice. That is why you want to have autonomy on the rover, but the greater help we can give it at a high level, the faster we can reach our goals and the fewer potential delays we’ll encounter.

This orbital view shows a region of complex Martian terrain that Perseverance could not navigate autonomously. The blue line shows the path that human planners estimated, while the white line shows the path taken by the rover. The inset image, from Perseverance’s hazard avoidance camera, shows the rocky, sandy, and sloped terrain.Source images: Olivier Toupet, Masahiro Ono, et al.; JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona/NASA

What happens when the autonomy system on Perseverance fails?

Maimone: We ended up not using the autonomy at all for about two months in more complex terrain while we tuned things and wrote new software to deal with that new terrain we hadn’t encountered before. Some of those changes were relatively quick, and some required months of study. For example, one parameter is the maximum amount of slope that the robot is allowed to climb, because on steep slopes, there is a risk of the rover slipping sideways.

We landed inside Jezero Crater, which was very flat, and so for the first three years, most of our driving was at less than 14 degrees of slope. When we finally decided to leave the crater, we began to encounter other terrain at higher tilts with greater rock density, and the experience we gained allowed us to re-tune the parameters to allow the rover to traverse those more difficult terrains, with slopes of up to 24 degrees.

Rover autonomy in the age of AI

Late last year, you let Anthropic’s Claude AI plan a 400-meter drive for Perseverance. How did that go?

Maimone: We had the AI look at the orbital images and pick out a path for us, which became the starting point of the day’s rover planning operations. Typically, that starting path comes from the human rover planner team, but in this case, it was generated by AI. Humans were still in the loop; the team reviewed it and made a couple of adjustments. AI gave us a solid starting point that allowed us to make rapid progress, because it’s much easier to validate a path than to pick one from scratch.

NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover took this selfie on July 23, 2024. The selfie is composed of 62 images taken by the WATSON (Wide Angle Topographic Sensor for Operations and eNgineering) camera on the end of the rover’s robotic arm.JPL-Caltech/MSSS/NASA

Do you think humans will remain a necessary part of rover operations, or do you see the next generation of Mars rovers operating for weeks at a time without human assistance?

Maimone: One of the things that has held us back from driving very long distances autonomously is that as we drive, the rover accumulates uncertainty in its position. When the uncertainty grows, it means we have to stay farther away from areas that human rover planners have identified as being potentially dangerous, called “keep-out zones.” In some cases, the uncertainty gets high enough that the rover can’t plan a safe path, because the keep-out zones (which grow with the rover’s uncertainty) get too big.

We now have a new capability that we’ve added to Perseverance called Mars Global Localization. With this new technology that can shrink our uncertainty, we theoretically have the ability to go as long as we have resources to keep driving safely based on our maps and keep-out zones.

But to truly run a mission for weeks, you need to not only drive long distances, but also execute science operations autonomously. We have people here also looking at automating science operations by doing image processing onboard the rover to get a better understanding of what’s out there and where to focus the instruments’ attention. So I do think we are getting to the point where we can support long-period autonomous operations. It has been a slow evolution, but we have great capabilities now and a good understanding of what’s needed to make it work well.

As someone who has been involved with all of these Mars rovers—including one that got stuck—do you fundamentally trust Perseverance to operate autonomously?

Maimone: I do. We built the software, tested it, ran millions of simulations, and did lots of work in the field in many different test environments. It hasn’t steered us wrong yet. We’re looking forward to setting even bigger records.

title: This Disembodied Hand Is All the Robot You Need
summary:
A hand attached to the end of an arm is a given for most humans, but what if robots didn’t have to play by the same rules as we do? Researchers from ETH Zurich have turned an off-the-shelf robotic hand into a completely self-contained robot that walks on its fingertips while using those same fingers to manipulate its environment.

Besides making the perfect Halloween accessory for anyone planning to dress up as a member of the Addams Family—who were famously accompanied by a disembodied walking hand called Thing—this robotic hand could make it possible to operate controls and handle objects in places a traditional robot arm can’t reach, the researchers say.

Soft Robotics Lab, ETH Zurich/YouTube

Amirhossein Kazemipour, a Ph.D. candidate in the Soft Robotics Lab at ETH Zurich who led the project, believes this hand could prove useful in contexts like fiddly maintenance tasks in industrial settings, or in search and rescue, where a robot could detach its hand to explore confined spaces too tight for the rest of its body. More broadly, he says, the work is a step toward a new approach to robotics in which body parts are not confined to a single role.

“I wanted to see how much a robotic hand could do without the rest of the robot,” Kazemipour told IEEE Spectrum. “Instead of having this traditional view of robotic parts, what if we could use those parts to do other tasks that they are not designed to do?”

This is not the first attempt to get a robot hand to walk, but previous work has typically relied on specially designed hands. The ETH team instead decided to use off-the-shelf hardware from Wuji Technology, augmented with an 80-gram backpack containing a battery, an inertial measurement unit (IMU), and a Raspberry Pi Zero. Kazemipour says they decided to go with a commercial robot hand because they didn’t want to compromise on the hand’s manipulation capabilities. This introduced significant challenges, he adds, because a hand’s shape is optimized for grasping rather than crawling.

How to Walk With Fingers

To teach the hand to walk, the researchers trained a model in simulation using reinforcement learning—an approach in which models learn skills through many rounds of trial and error, receiving rewards for getting closer to the desired behavior along with penalties when they diverge from it. But Kazemipour says the unusual geometry of a hand meant they couldn’t just reuse methods used to train other kinds of legged robots. Standard quadrupeds or bipeds tend to be symmetrical on their left and right sides, which simplifies walking and balance, he says. Hands, in contrast, are not at all symmetrical, with fingers of different lengths and an opposable thumb.

In addition to rewards for moving at the right speed and in the right direction and penalties for things like wobbling or jerky movement, the team introduced a novel way to keep the hand in a crawling stance during the simulated training. To account for unequal digit length, they gave each finger its own target position relative to the palm, based on where it naturally sits when in the crawling posture. They then penalized the fingers for straying too far from that reference point, creating what they describe as “virtual springs” that pull the fingers back to the crawling stance. Crucially, the penalties for fingers moving forward and backward are significantly less than those for moving side to side, so taking steps in that way costs the hand very little compared with the rewards it receives for moving.

The team also trained separate models for skills like righting the hand when it falls over, pressing keys on a keyboard, and pushing objects to a target. All four models fit on the onboard computer, says Kazemipour, and the controller can switch between them as necessary. In real-world tests, the hand crawled across 14 different surfaces including smooth floors, metal grates, grass, and gravel. Other experiments confirmed that it could make both right and left turns, and hit an average speed of 9 centimeters per second. The hand was able to right itself in 21 of 25 trials. When given a video feed from an overhead camera, it even managed to autonomously push a 41-gram cube to targets up to 40 cm away 15 times in a row.

“What interests me most about this work is that the same fingers can move the hand, support its weight, and interact with its surroundings,” says Masahiko Inami, a professor at the University of Tokyo whose group has developed hand-shaped walking robots. He agrees that a mobile hand could be useful for reaching confined spaces and operating controls that an entire arm could not easily access, though he says practical deployment would require onboard perception and more robust navigation. Hideki Shimobayashi, a Ph.D. student in Inami’s lab, also points out that walking puts very different loads on a hand compared to grasping, so durability may be a challenge.

However, Matei Ciocarlie, an associate professor of mechanical engineering at Columbia University, says it’s a “cool result” that suggests robot hands don’t have to be restricted to the same capabilities as their human counterparts. “One can imagine an entirely new class of mobile manipulators that are simultaneously dexterous, able to traverse complex terrain, and able to manipulate payloads comparable in size to themselves,” he says.

Kazemipour sees his work as part of a longer-term vision for robots made up of parts that are not tied to a single job or even a single body plan, something he calls “autonomous modular embodiments.” “Robotic body parts should not be permanently assigned to a single function,” he says. “They can dynamically transition between roles, between being components of one embodiment system and autonomous agents, according to the task.”

title: Atlas Robot’s New Hand May Outperform Humanlike Designs
summary:
Today, Boston Dynamics is announcing a redesigned hand for its Atlas robot. The previous generation could do some crazy superhuman things with its three fingers, but it was never intended for mass production in the tens or hundreds of thousands. Switching from research hardware to a scalable product makes previously ignorable questions suddenly paramount: How can you make a hand that does everything you need it to do but is also rugged and reliable and cost-effective? It’s questions like these that drove the design of the new Atlas hand, and while it doesn’t look much like a human hand, it might be a hand that makes it out into the real world.

- YouTube www.youtube.com

Compared to the almost eerily humanlike hands designed by a litany of other humanoid robotics companies, Atlas’s new hand does look awfully clunky. We’ve certainly seen some of those robots with much more humanlike hands perform dexterous manipulation tasks that are, speaking as someone who has personally witnessed robots haplessly fumble their way through the world for nearly two decades now, nothing short of incredible. And it’s not just what these hands can do—it’s how they look while doing it, as slim, graceful mechanical copies of our own hands. They seem like science fiction, and to some extent, that’s exactly what they are.

“Hands are a ruthless design trade-off,” Alberto Rodriguez, director of robot behavior at Boston Dynamics, tells IEEE Spectrum. “There’s no way around it, you’re always giving up on something. And many of the current designs are giving up on things like reliability and manufacturability.” This is what invariably happens when you try and cram everything necessary to make a robotic hand function within the form factor of a human hand: It’s going to be either very fragile or very expensive, and likely both at the same time. The unfortunate reality is that for now, and likely for the immediate future, all that these sorts of hands are good for are research and demos.

With Atlas’s new hand, Boston Dynamics is making the design trade-offs necessary to achieve a hand that, according to the press release, is capable of a vast array of useful tasks, including using tools; is strong and rugged; can be cleanly simulated; can be mass-manufactured and repaired at reliably low cost; and is close enough in form factor to a human hand that human demonstrations can be used to train it.

You’ll notice that “looks cosmetically like a human hand” is nowhere on that list, and this new hand doesn’t. Rodriguez explains that getting rid of the pinky was a straightforward decision, agreed on after his team spent a day with their pinkies taped to their ring fingers. But why even add a fourth finger, when the previous generation of Atlas’ hand seemed to do well with only three? It’s not just the extra finger, but a complete redesign that almost doubled the degrees of freedom between the old hand and the new, going from 7 to 13.

Boston Dynamics

“We also added the ability for the fingers to splay open because we knew that it was important for one finger to be able to move against another, and we also knew that we needed to be able to hold the handle of a tool with a trigger,” Rodriguez says, which includes many common tools like drills or welding torches. “We’re convinced that from a product perspective, this hand should be able to do everything we need it to do for the foreseeable horizon.” And that ability to finger splay goes beyond what human hands are capable of. According to Rodriguez, “With reinforcement learning, we can discover uses for these superhuman extra motions and exploit them.”

Reliability, manufacturability, and cost are all closely related. By reducing the degrees of freedom relative to other more anthropomorphic hand designs down to just 13, Boston Dynamics can use fewer, larger, and more powerful actuators. The actuators are embedded directly into the joints themselves in a direct-drive configuration, with a transmission that allows the motors to be back-driven and react to force and contact. Each actuator pack is a single unit that can be easily replaced, and there are no delicate tendons or cables across joints to stretch and break. “What we’re working on right now is figuring out what needs to change in the fine details of our design if we want to make 100,000 of these hands a year,” Rodriguez says.

Not every humanoid company will make the trade-offs that Boston Dynamics has done here, and there’s still plenty of room for creativity when it comes to hand design. But if humanoids with hands are going to scale, some difficult decisions will have to be made, and it’ll take some compromise to deliver on the promises that the humanoid industry has committed to.

title: Mexican EPICS in IEEE Team Builds Portable Educational Platform
summary:
In Guadalajara, Mexico, many high schools have motivated teachers and talented students with an interest in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics, but they lack access to advanced tools such as robotics laboratories. The resources shortfall limits the students’ opportunities for hands-on learning on cutting-edge applications.

A team from ITESO, Universidad Jesuita de Guadalajara, is working to change that. Through the EPICS in IEEE initiative, a multidisciplinary group of 15 engineering students, faculty advisors, and IEEE Guadalajara Section volunteers developed RoboMeshA. The portable, self-contained educational platform brings robotics and AI experiences into classrooms.

EPICS is administered by IEEE Educational Activities and funded by the IEEE Robotics and Automation Society.

A mobile laboratory

Rather than requiring a school to build a dedicated computer lab or install complex software, RoboMeshA operates as an all-in-one mobile learning network.

“RoboMeshA brings robotics and AI to students who don’t have access to specialized facilities or preinstalled software,” says team member Fernando Vidal Luna, an IEEE student member and a mechatronics engineering major at ITESO.

Students connect directly to the platform from a user-friendly web browser. They can interact with the robot manually or use its control modes to watch it move and detect and avoid obstacles.

“The project combines mechanical design, embedded systems, control engineering, computer vision, and AI into a single robotic system that functions as a mobile learning laboratory,” says faculty advisor Jorge A. Lizarraga.

The team says young students are interested in technology, programming, and robotics but don’t have an opportunity to work with systems that combine mechanics, electronics, software, and control.

“RoboMeshA allows students to see how all these disciplines work together in a tangible and understandable way,” says team member José S. González, who also is studying mechatronics engineering.

The team has built two units and is developing a modular coupling framework to expand the system’s capabilities for research and classroom demonstrations. The structured system design approach connects independent software components while minimizing internal dependencies, enabling four RobotMeshA robots to operate together.

Overcoming design challenges

The team faced significant hurdles while designing the project.

“One key challenge involved the robot’s structural design,” Luna says. “It wasn’t only about making a chassis where all the components fit and the design had sufficient stability, rigidity, and weight distribution. It was also about ensuring that the electronics were protected while still being accessible for maintenance, testing, and modifications.”

“It was also challenging to design a platform that could be used by students with different levels of experience,” González adds.

“When students realize the technology they develop can inspire others and improve lives, engineering becomes far more meaningful.” —Luis Fernando Luque-Vega

The team partnered with the CETI Colomos and Prepa ITESO high schools to validate the platform in classroom settings.

“We wanted the first interactions with the robot to be simple and intuitive,” González says, “such that students could simply power the robot, connect to its network, and begin interacting with it, rather than having to deal with software installation, extensive configuration, or troubleshooting.”

Engineering with social impact

Many of the students who participated were from ITESO’s applied professional projects program. The experience offered them practical training in project management, system integration, and user-centered design.

The team also presented a research paper and a project poster in May at the Engineering Congress of the Jesuit University System.

“Seeing a design move from a digital model to a physical system was invaluable,” González says. “Working with students from different backgrounds taught us to listen to end users and design for their actual needs.”

Project lead Luis Fernando Luque-Vega, an IEEE member, says he’d like the venture to serve as a blueprint for engineering education.

“I hope RoboMeshA is adopted by schools, universities, and IEEE student branches across Mexico and internationally as a model for integrating technical innovation with community engagement,” Luque-Vega says.

By pairing engineering talent with community service, initiatives such as EPICS in IEEE demonstrate how targeted support can turn academic concepts into real-world solutions.

“When students realize the technology they develop can inspire others and improve lives, engineering becomes far more meaningful,” Luque-Vega says.

For more information on service-learning opportunities, visit the EPICS website.

title: Barbara Mazzolai Wants to Build a New Field of Robotics
summary:
Throughout her career, roboticist Barbara Mazzolai has turned to nature for inspiration. Now she wants to ensure the technology she builds gives back to the environment, too.

After starting her career as a biologist, a chance opportunity saw Mazzolai switch streams to engineering and become an early pioneer of bioinspired robotics. Building on her knowledge of biology’s ability to solve a diverse set of problems, she has developed robots based on octopuses, plant roots, and even seeds. “I’ve always been fascinated by living organisms, [and] by the extraordinary variety of solutions in nature, selected by the evolutionary process,” she says.

Barbara Mazzolai


Employer:

Italian Institute of Technology

Occupation:

Associate director for robotics; director of the Bioinspired Soft Robotics Laboratory

Education:

Master’s degree in biology, University of Pisa; master’s degree in eco-management and audit schemes, Scuola Superiore Sant’Anna; Ph.D. in microsystems engineering, University of Rome Tor Vergata

But Mazzolai, now the associate director for robotics at the Italian Institute of Technology, in Genoa, also believes engineering needs to reckon with its own impact on the natural world. That’s why she is advocating for a new field of research she calls “sustainability robotics.”

In a manifesto published in Nature Machine Intelligence in July, she and her collaborators outline a vision for a new approach to designing robots that’s meant to improve the relationship between nature, humanity, and technology.

“We need to reduce the footprint of our technology,” she says. “It’s really about thinking in a different way to open new possibilities for robotics [and] for society.” In this new mode of thinking, Mazzolai considers sustainability a core component of the design.

A child of nature

Mazzolai traces her fascination with the living world back to her childhood growing up on Italy’s Tuscan coast, close to the port city Livorno. Her father was a public-health inspector and a professional mycologist, and the family spent a lot of time exploring forests and learning about the local fungi and plants.

After toying with the prospect of pursuing art, her other major passion, Mazzolai ultimately decided to enroll at the University of Pisa in 1987 to study biology. She was particularly drawn to marine biology, but shortly before graduating with a master’s degree in 1995, she secured a research position at the Italian National Research Council’s Institute of Biophysics studying the cycles of heavy metals like mercury through both living and nonliving parts of the environment.

This involved collecting and analyzing samples from water, soil, vegetables, and even humans to understand the impact these metals have on health and the environment. She balanced this work with studying environmental management at the Scuola Superiore Sant’Anna, in Pisa, graduating with a master’s degree in 1998.

During that time, however, she learned that the university was recruiting biologists to help design new devices for environmental monitoring. She applied for and got the job in 1999 and began working as a research assistant under renowned bioroboticist Paolo Dario, first developing sensors and then robots meant to monitor air, water, and soil.

Even before entering a doctoral program, Mazzolai was promoted to assistant professor in 2004 and shortly afterward made her first foray into bioinspired robotics. In collaboration with colleagues at Sant’Anna, she helped design a soft robot inspired by the octopus. “We proposed it as a paradigm for launching this idea of soft robotics: demonstrating that [robots] can be soft, but at the same time apply strong force to the environment, like the animal does,” she says.

Back to school

In 2007 Mazzolai enrolled in a Ph.D. in microsystems engineering at Tor Vergata University of Rome, which she balanced with her role at Sant’Anna. She was already relying heavily on microfabrication techniques to develop sensors for her robots, and she was keen to push that part of the field forward.

While robots frequently feature sensors designed for perception, such as tactile or proprioceptive sensors, these systems typically focus on understanding the robot’s position in its environment, she says. “But there are few robots that integrate physical or chemical sensors to really understand the environment they move in,” she adds.

“I’ve always been fascinated by living organisms, [and] by the extraordinary variety of solutions in nature.”

Mazzolai was appointed as a team leader at the Center for Micro-BioRobotics of the Italian Institute of Technology in 2009, where she continued her work on the emerging field of bioinspired robotics. Two years later, she completed her Ph.D. and was promoted to director of the center.

Planting the seeds

Around this time Mazzolai says she became interested in using plants as a model for new kinds of robots, expanding bioinspiration beyond just animals. In particular, she was captivated by the ability of roots to efficiently explore the underground environment, and she imagined machines with the same deftness could have applications in both environmental modeling and precision agriculture.

While many bioinspired robots mimic animals, plants also serve as a muse for Mazzolai. This tendril-like bot can coil around other structures like a vine. Italian Institute of Technology

When she first proposed the idea, colleagues were somewhat skeptical of robots based on seemingly static organisms. But in reality, she says, plants move nonstop through a process known as indeterminate growth. “They really grow for their entire life,” she says. “They adapt their morphology, their behavior to the external environment; they repair, they sense, they communicate.”

Trying to mimic a system that operates on such different principles to conventional robotics required some serious thinking, however. Mazzolai says that working in bioinspired robotics sometimes requires you to have “two separate brains”—one of a biologist and one of an engineer.

The process often involves deep study of the target organism to learn the underlying principles that shape how it operates before trying to engineer a robot capable of mimicking them. “It’s not a copy of natural organisms,” says Mazzolai, because a living organism is both difficult to replicate and has different goals.

In the case of plant roots, what makes them so efficient at exploring the soil is that they reduce friction by growing only at the very fine tip of the structure, while the thicker base of the root remains static. This significantly reduces the amount of energy required to push through the earth compared to that of a more conventional drill, which must push the entire structure from above.

To realize this principle in a robot, her team developed a miniaturized 3D printer that sits at the machine’s tip and feeds thermoplastic filament through a heated nozzle to build a snakelike body behind it. This allows the robot to push through the soil efficiently. The tip also contains sensors that allow it to avoid obstacles and detect nearby nutrients or water.

Making robotics sustainable

After spending so much of her career borrowing from nature, Mazzolai is now eager to return the favor. Many modern technologies, including plastics and car batteries, have been developed with little thought about how they will affect the environment at the end of their life cycles, she says.

She wants to ensure that robotics doesn’t follow the same path. This is the inspiration for what she and collaborators now call sustainability robotics. The approach has three central pillars: ensuring that robots have minimal impact on the environment; that they’re available to people from across the world and all socioeconomic backgrounds; and that they’re “symbiotic,” providing benefits to both humans and nature.

More concretely, Mazzolai would like to incorporate the concept of a life cycle into the design of robots, so that at the end of their useful life these machines can be reused, recycled, or even biodegraded.

While that might sound ambitious, she’s confident that all the ingredients to make it a reality are in place. And it’s a vision that she is certain will inspire future roboticists. “There are younger people who want to really work in this field because this is the future, their future,” she says. Facing the threat of ongoing environmental damage, “they want to develop something that can help.”

NYU Tandon researchers built an undulatory robot that pumps water between its head and tail to climb slopes, clear steps, and swim, all while keeping the same basic gait.

On an incline, shifting water toward the head increases the force pressing the robot’s front contact points against the surface, giving them more traction. Head-biased placement was the only configuration that successfully carried WorMa up the steepest incline tested, 19.5 degrees; every other configuration slid back down. It also reduced the robot’s cost of transport by at least 33 percent compared with the other configurations.
Steps required something different. Neither a fixed head-heavy nor tail-heavy robot could clear a step on its own. The researchers instead had WorMa approach the step with water in its head for traction, then shifted the water to the tail and raised the head and neck so the tail could push the robot closer. Once the head anchored on the step’s edge, the water shifted back to the head, and the robot continued. That sequence got WorMa over steps as high as 15 centimeters.

Legged robots are versatile on land, but their use in underwater environments remains limited. Extending quadruped locomotion to water enables amphibious mobility with applications in inspection, environmental monitoring, and disaster response. This paper presents the design, modeling, and experimental validation of a reproducible underwater quadruped robot. The robot is built around custom waterproof motor housings machined from polyoxymethylene plastic, which use off-the-shelf O-rings and dynamic shaft seals. A simplified model is derived to describe the dynamics of this underwater legged system, capturing how drag forces on spherical end effectors transmit torque to the floating base. Building on this model, a closed-loop attitude controller is developed using an error formulation defined on the special orthogonal group SO(3). The controller is evaluated both in simulation and experimentally in a water tank, where the robot tracks desired orientation setpoints in roll, pitch, and yaw.

This CMU Robotics Institute Seminar is by Erol Şahin from METU, on “Augmenting Bee Colonies with Robotics and AI Technologies for Ecosystem Support.”

Earth’s ecosystems are facing a rapid decline in biodiversity, with honeybees—keystone pollinators critical to ecosystem stability—being among the most affected. The EU-funded RoboRoyale project addresses this crisis by integrating advanced robotics and AI to augment the beehive, enabling observation at unprecedented resolutions and scales. Featured on the cover of Science Robotics and receiving the 6th Edge of Government Award at the World Government Summit in 2024, our system tracks the Queen’s behaviors, colony efficiency, comb states, and long-term foraging activities, while advancing microrobotic intervention capabilities to support hive health. In this talk, I will discuss the challenges of developing this system, share key findings regarding complex social interactions, and explore the future potential of bio-hybrid research.
